narrator.instruct: Gripping, energetic storyteller telling an amazing piece of history, brisk and excited, never calm.

villager.instruct: Outraged village woman, loud and indignant, comic disbelief.

merchant.instruct: Startled merchant tumbling off his horse, shouting in protest.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Marco Polo wrote that the Khan's letters raced two hundred miles in a day. Yet no single horse made the trip.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: His riders went bound in tight bands, their belts jingling with bells.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: But a horse at full gallop tires long before sunset.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So every twenty-five miles, the Khan built a station called a Yam.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Some kept four hundred horses, half saddled, half out at grass.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Polo counted over ten thousand stations and three hundred thousand horses.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And who supplied all those horses? The villages next door.

lines.speaker: villager
lines.text: Four hundred horses? I have three goats!

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Every rider also carried a paiza, a metal tablet with a falcon.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: If his horse broke down, anyone he met had to hand over theirs.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You see, no horse ran far. Only the letter did.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The bells rang out long before the rider arrived.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So the next station saddled a fresh horse, and a clerk wrote down the time.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The letter changed hands at a gallop and never stopped.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Fruit picked one morning in the capital reached the Khan the next evening, ten days' journey away.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Every horse got tired. The letter never did.
